title: Practice Set DM4 — Type Casting and Coercion
description: Recognition track: type casting and coercion. String → int edge cases, dates that were strings all along. Companion to the Foundations Casting chapter.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings (10–20 rows depending on exercise). Most exercises use a smaller inline sample shown in the Evidence panel; this file is the schema-level reference.
Substations reference (6 rows). Used in cleaning + type-casting exercises.

tasks.title: Cast '12.5' To Int — What Happens?

description.context: Casting a string-typed column to integer is one of the most common cleanup steps, and three popular engines disagree on what to do when the input string contains a fractional part like '12.5'. Pandas .astype(int) is STRICT — it routes through Python's int() built-in, which rejects '12.5' with a ValueError because int() refuses to silently truncate. DuckDB's CAST(... AS INT) is LENIENT — it truncates toward zero and returns 12. PySpark's .cast('int') is SAFE-NULL — it returns null for any value it cannot parse cleanly, keeping the pipeline running but losing the value. Three engines, three recovery strategies for the same input.
description.task: What does each idiom produce for the value '12.5'?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 3-row sample showing a string column daily_kw_str that includes the value '12.5'.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms for casting daily_kw_str to integer.

# Idiom A — Pandas .astype(int)
result_a = df['daily_kw_str'].astype(int)

# Idiom B — SQL CAST AS INT (DuckDB on the same data)
# SELECT CAST(daily_kw_str AS INT) FROM df

# Idiom C — PySpark .cast('int')
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
result_c = spark_df.withColumn('daily_kw_int', col('daily_kw_str').cast('int'))

fields.label: What does each idiom produce for the value '12.5'?
options: All three engines produce 12 — every standard integer cast truncates the fractional part toward zero. Pandas, DuckDB, and PySpark are interchangeable here; the cast is universal and consistent.
All three engines produce 13 — banker's rounding (IEEE 754) applies during integer casts: .5 rounds to the nearest even integer, and 13 is the result for all three engines.

Pandas .astype(int) raises ValueError ('invalid literal for int() with base 10'), DuckDB CAST returns 12 (truncates toward zero), PySpark .cast('int') silently returns null. Three engines, three recovery strategies.
Pandas .astype(int) returns 12 by truncating, DuckDB CAST raises a conversion error refusing the value, and PySpark .cast('int') returns 13 by rounding.
fields.correctAnswer: Pandas .astype(int) raises ValueError ('invalid literal for int() with base 10'), DuckDB CAST returns 12 (truncates toward zero), PySpark .cast('int') silently returns null. Three engines, three recovery strategies.
fields.rationale: The three engines disagree on '12.5'. Pandas .astype(int) routes through Python's int() built-in which refuses to silently lose precision and raises ValueError. DuckDB CAST AS INT truncates toward zero, returning 12. PySpark .cast('int') is the safe-null variant — it returns null on parse failure to keep streaming pipelines running, but the bad value vanishes without a warning. The most common Junior confusion is assuming 'cast to int' is a single universal operation; in reality each engine picked a different point on the strict-vs-lenient spectrum.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes all int casts truncate. Pandas does not — it raises rather than silently truncate.

Option B: Applies floating-point banker's rounding to int casts. Int casts truncate or fail; they do not round.

Option D: Names the right engines but assigns the wrong behaviors — easy mistake when each engine documents this differently.

tasks.crossReference: Foundations curriculum: Casting chapter, 'Engine-specific cast failure modes' section. Tool-specific extensions: Pandas Junior Recognition Track PJR6.1 (errors='coerce' parameter that aligns Pandas with PySpark's silent-null behavior); PySpark Junior Recognition Track PJSR3.4 (the .cast() vs .try_cast() distinction).

tasks.title: The Date That Was A String All Along

description.context: A column whose name contains the word 'date' is not necessarily of dtype datetime — it can still be plain string (object dtype). When you compare a string column against a string literal in Pandas, the comparison is LEXICOGRAPHIC: Pandas walks the two strings character by character and compares Unicode code points, stopping at the first difference. This works correctly for date comparison ONLY if every value is the same fixed-width ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD with zero-padded month and day). The moment a value has unpadded digits ('2026-01-9' instead of '2026-01-09'), the position of the digits no longer matches across rows and the lexicographic comparison gives wrong answers — even though the strings 'look like dates'.
description.task: Why does M-002 with date '2026-01-9' pass a filter for `>= '2026-01-10'`?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 5-row sample. Note the `date` column is stored as STRING despite its name, with mixed formatting: most values are zero-padded ('2026-01-15'), but one row (M-002) has unpadded day ('2026-01-9') from a different upstream source.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# The filter intent: keep meter readings dated on or after 2026-01-10.
result = df[df['date'] >= '2026-01-10']

# Result row count: 5 (all rows pass — including M-002 from January 9)
# Specification: keep ONLY rows from January 10 onward.

fields.label: Why does M-002 with date '2026-01-9' pass a filter for `>= '2026-01-10'`?
options: The date column holds strings; comparison is lexicographic. At position 8, '2026-01-9' has '9' and '2026-01-10' has '1' — '9' has a higher Unicode code point than '1', so the row passes >= '2026-01-10'. Fix: pd.to_datetime first.

Pandas applies date semantics regardless of column dtype, but the locale parses the threshold '2026-01-10' as YYYY-DD-MM (so it becomes October 1, 2026) and the row passes because every January date is before October.

Pandas auto-coerces both sides to datetime when a string column is compared to a string literal, but the coercion silently fails on the unpadded '2026-01-9' and the row is treated as null and retained by the >= operator.

The >= operator on string columns uses an internal numeric encoding that maps each character to its Unicode position; the resulting integer comparison is mathematically equivalent to the date comparison the teammate intended.
fields.correctAnswer: The date column holds strings; comparison is lexicographic. At position 8, '2026-01-9' has '9' and '2026-01-10' has '1' — '9' has a higher Unicode code point than '1', so the row passes >= '2026-01-10'. Fix: pd.to_datetime first.
fields.rationale: The values in the date column are strings (object dtype) despite the column name. df['date'] >= '2026-01-10' is a lexicographic string comparison, not a date comparison. The first 8 characters '2026-01-' match; at position 8 the row has '9' (Unicode 57) while the threshold has '1' (Unicode 49), so the row compares as greater. Lexicographic comparison only matches date semantics when every value is fixed-width zero-padded ISO. The most common Junior confusion is assuming a column named 'date' has datetime semantics — only the dtype determines that, not the name. Always cast with pd.to_datetime before comparing.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a locale-driven date-parsing on string-vs-string comparisons. Pandas does no such parsing here.

Option C: Believes Pandas auto-coerces strings to dates and treats parse failures as null. It does neither — string-on-string stays string-on-string.

Option D: Claims lexicographic comparison equals date comparison. Only true on fixed-width zero-padded ISO; breaks on '2026-01-9'.
